Technical Guide

Selecting a PTFE Gasket

PTFE gaskets seal almost any chemical — but only if the gasket construction suits the flange, the bolt load and the temperature. Here is how to match them.

PTFE is the default gasket material wherever the media is corrosive or purity matters. But “PTFE gasket” covers several quite different constructions, and the most common cause of a leaking PTFE joint is not chemical attack — it is a gasket that has crept, lost its bolt load or failed to seat on the flange it was fitted to.

The four main types of PTFE gasket

General comparison. Performance depends on the specific product, thickness and installation — use the gasket data sheet for design values.
Gasket typeStrengthsLimitationsTypical use
Solid virgin PTFE
skived or moulded sheet		Widest chemical resistance; high purity; simple to cutCreeps and relaxes under bolt load, especially when hot; limited conformabilityLow-pressure, near-ambient chemical and hygienic joints
Filled / restructured PTFE sheetMuch lower creep and better bolt-load retention than solid virginFiller sets the chemical limits; needs adequate bolt load to seatGeneral process piping on steel raised-face flanges
Expanded PTFE (ePTFE)Very soft and conformable; seals at low bolt load; fills surface damageThins considerably on compression; needs suitable bolt load and correct handlingGlass-lined, FRP, plastic-lined and uneven or damaged flanges
Envelope gasket
PTFE jacket over an insert		PTFE faces the media while the insert provides resilienceInsert must not be exposed to media; jacket can be damaged by poor fit-upGlass-lined and enamelled equipment, large or fragile flanges

Solid virgin PTFE

Cut from skived or moulded PTFE sheet, solid virgin gaskets offer the broadest chemical resistance and the highest purity. Their weakness is creep: under bolt load the PTFE slowly flows outwards, the gasket thins and bolt load falls. This gets worse as temperature rises. Solid virgin gaskets suit low-pressure joints near ambient temperature, or joints where the gasket is confined, for example in a tongue-and-groove or spigot-and-recess flange.

Filled and restructured PTFE sheet

Adding fillers — common examples are silica, barium sulphate and glass microspheres — and processing the sheet to create a more stable structure greatly reduces creep and improves bolt-load retention. These sheets are the usual choice for steel raised-face flanges in process piping. The filler governs chemical suitability: for example, silica- and glass-based fillers are not suited to hydrofluoric acid or hot strong alkalis. Always check the specific sheet against your media.

Expanded PTFE (ePTFE)

Expanded PTFE is stretched during manufacture to create a soft, microporous, fibrous structure. It compresses readily, seals at low seating stress and flows into scratches, pits and waviness in the flange face. That makes it a strong choice for fragile or imperfect flanges. It is supplied as sheet for cut gaskets and as tape or cord that can be formed in place on large or non-standard flanges. Expect a large reduction in thickness on compression, and follow the supplier’s installation guidance.

Envelope gaskets

An envelope gasket has a thin PTFE jacket wrapped around a compressible insert, such as a fibre-based or elastomeric sheet, sometimes with a metal reinforcement. The PTFE provides chemical resistance at the wetted inner edge and faces; the insert provides the resilience that solid PTFE lacks. Envelope gaskets are widely used on glass-lined vessels and large equipment flanges. The insert must be fully protected from the media, so the envelope’s inner diameter must match the bore and the gasket must be centred correctly.

Matching the gasket to the service

Media

Virgin PTFE handles virtually all process chemicals, with a small number of known exceptions. With filled sheets and envelope gaskets, check the filler or insert as well. Include cleaning and flushing chemicals, not just the process stream. Our chemical resistance guide has the details.

Temperature

PTFE’s continuous service range extends to approximately 260 °C, but creep and bolt-load loss increase as temperature rises. At elevated temperature, restructured sheet or ePTFE generally holds load better than solid virgin PTFE. Thermal cycling is harder on a joint than steady temperature, because PTFE’s high thermal expansion causes the gasket stress to rise and fall with each cycle.

Pressure

Higher pressure demands better blow-out resistance and bolt-load retention. Thinner gaskets and confined designs perform better than thick, unconfined ones. For higher-pressure duty, filled or restructured sheet is usually preferred to solid virgin PTFE. Consider hydrostatic test pressure as well as operating pressure.

Flange type and condition

Flange type / conditionWhat it needsGasket types to consider
Steel raised-face, good conditionGood bolt-load retention and blow-out resistanceFilled / restructured PTFE sheet; solid PTFE for mild duty
Steel flat-faceFull-face gasket so the bolt load does not bend the flangesFull-face filled PTFE sheet or ePTFE
Glass-lined or enamelledLow seating stress; conforms to waviness without point loadsEnvelope gaskets with a soft insert; ePTFE
FRP or plasticSeals at low bolt load so flanges are not cracked or distortedePTFE or soft envelope gaskets; full-face where appropriate
Damaged, pitted or warpedHigh conformability to fill irregularitiesePTFE, or thicker soft gaskets — repair the flange where possible

Bolt load and creep relaxation

Every gasket needs enough compressive stress to seat it and enough remaining stress in service to keep it sealed. PTFE complicates this because it relaxes: some of the bolt load applied at assembly is lost over the following hours as the gasket creeps. Good practice includes:

  • Using the thinnest gasket the flange condition allows. Thinner gaskets creep less and resist blow-out better.
  • Tightening in a cross pattern in several stages to compress the gasket evenly.
  • Re-tightening after an initial settling period, before the system is pressurised or heated, where the gasket supplier and your bolting procedure allow it.
  • Respecting the flange’s limits. Glass-lined and FRP flanges can be damaged by excessive bolt load; choose a gasket that seals within the torque the flange can safely take.
  • Using lubricated, well-maintained bolting so applied torque translates into consistent bolt load.

Dimensional standards

For standard pipe flanges, gasket dimensions are commonly specified by reference to published standards — for example ASME B16.21 for non-metallic flat gaskets on ASME flanges, and EN 1514-1 for non-metallic flat gaskets on PN-designated flanges. Quote the standard, nominal size and pressure class or PN rating, and say whether you need a ring (inside-bolt-circle) gasket or a full-face gasket with bolt holes. For non-standard flanges, a dimensioned drawing or a sample is best. These standards are references for dimensions; they do not by themselves define the material or its suitability for your service.

Checklist for specifying a PTFE gasket

  1. Flange — standard, nominal size and class or PN; or ID, OD, bolt-hole count, diameter and PCD.
  2. Style — ring or full-face; flat, raised-face, tongue-and-groove or other.
  3. Flange material and condition — steel, glass-lined, FRP, plastic; any damage or waviness.
  4. Gasket type and grade — solid virgin, filled or restructured, ePTFE or envelope (with insert material).
  5. Thickness — and any tolerance that matters.
  6. Media — all chemicals with concentrations, including cleaning agents.
  7. Temperature — normal, maximum and whether it cycles.
  8. Pressure — operating and test.
  9. Bolting — size, number, material and the torque the flange allows.
  10. Quantity — and whether it is a one-off or repeat requirement.

Gasket selection affects safety. Final selection, bolt loads and installation procedure should be confirmed by the responsible engineer using the gasket supplier’s data and your plant’s bolting procedures.
